equivalents.note: The Tibetan names the melody chen po, 'great', in the place of the rāga name Gavaṛā; the word does not render the name, and why it stands there is unclear.
The Tibetan has stegs bu, 'stand, platform', as for Munidatta's pīṭhaka in the commentary (cp.02.m2), and construes the line as 'the stand cannot be held' (gzung du med).
The Tibetan names a fruit, bse yab, whose identification is uncertain, and adds 'bras bu, 'fruit': 'the crocodile eats the bse yab, the fruit of the tree'.
Rigs ngan, 'low-born woman', with the vocative kye for bho, implies that the translators read the word as vijātī; the commentary's lemma is the same (cp.02.m3).
The verse reads sgo bdun, 'seven doors', probably a slip for sgo mdun, 'in front of the door', which is the commentary's lemma for aṅgana (cp.02.m3).
The Tibetan has khang bzhugs, 'staying in the house', which may be its rendering of the unclear second element of gharapaṇa.
The Tibetan phrase seems to name a part of the house (khang logs, 'side of the house') rather than an ear ornament, so the translators probably read or construed kāneṭa differently.
The Tibetan has sgyug mo, 'mother-in-law', here and in the commentary's lemma (cp.02.m4), so it may reflect a different reading (compare Old Bengali sāsu, 'mother-in-law').
The line shortens the word to rkun, apparently for the metre, where the refrain has rkun mas.
The Tibetan has glu, 'song', for caryā; the commentary's Tibetan calls it spyod pa'i glu, 'song of conduct' (cp.02.m6).
For kāyavṛkṣa, 'body-tree', the commentary uses ljon shing where the verse line has ljon pa (cp.02.1b).
In the Tibetan, bodhicitta falls from (las) the vajra jewel, where the Sanskrit has it fall into it (locative vajramaṇau).
The commentary's lemma sgo mdun, 'in front of the door', suggests that the verse's sgo bdun, 'seven doors' (cp.02.2a), is a slip.
Here the Tibetan transcribes dhru(va) and adds rkang pa, 'verse', instead of translating it as brtan pa'i rkang pa.
The Tibetan has sna tshogs pa'i dga' ba, 'joy of variety', where the Sanskrit has viramānanda, 'joy of cessation', so it may have read a different word (sna tshogs usually renders vicitra).
The commentary has rkun po where the refrain has rkun ma (cp.02.2b).
The Tibetan calls it the yogic sleep of 'the joy of peace' (zhi ba'i dga' ba), where the Sanskrit has 'the fourth joy' (caturthānanda).
The Tibetan has no word for kāya, 'body', and puts the person of time in the agent case (dus kyi skyes bus), where the Sanskrit has the dative of fearing (kāyakālapuruṣāya).
The Tibetan attaches wisdom-knowledge to the avadhūtī in a genitive (shes rab ye shes kyi rang bzhin rnam par dag pa'i), not as the instrument of the empowerment (prajñājñānena).
In the Tibetan the avadhūtī emanates (sprul) the three worlds 'in the form of conventional bodhicitta', where the Sanskrit has 'conventionally, in the form of semen' (saṃvṛtyā śukrarūpeṇa).
The Tibetan renders niṣprapañca without the intensifier atīva, 'utterly'.
The commentary renders caryā as spyod pa'i glu, 'song of conduct', which accounts for the bare glu, 'song', of the verse line (cp.02.5a).
The Tibetan translates nirañjana literally, 'without eye-salve', and renders līna, 'absorbed', as mi snang 'gyur, 'becomes invisible'.

questions: thief, cp.02.m3: no equivalent given. The Tibetan turns 'stolen by the thief, innate joy' (sahajānandacaureṇa hṛtaṃ) into 'innate joy steals' (lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' bas rku bar byed), with the verb rku and no noun for the thief.

Not a term match, but worth checking: in cp.02.m2 the Tibetan explains du li as du = gnyid kyi rnam pa, 'the aspect of sleep', where the Sanskrit has dvayākāra, 'the dual aspect'; gnyid is probably a slip for gnyis, 'two'.
